title: Running a Chess YouTube Channel entirely by AI — Stephan Steinfurt, TNG
talk_summary: Stephan Steinfurt describes a fully automated pipeline that downloads Lichess games nightly, has a tool-equipped LLM agent (Gemini 3 Pro) analyze positions using legal-move, board-simulation, engine, and checks/captures/threats tools, then renders narrated videos via 11 Labs TTS and auto-uploads to YouTube. The key architectural lesson is deliberately giving the reasoning model tools and letting it do the thinking rather than pre-computing analysis in scripts, at ~20-30 cents per video with roughly a 1-in-20 error rate.

takeaways.technique: Give the reasoning model tools instead of pre-computed analysis scripts
takeaways.what_they_do: They replaced Python scripts that assembled position analysis and passed it to the LLM with an agent that calls tools itself (legal moves, board play/undo, engine eval, checks-captures-threats) and reasons over the results.

takeaways.technique: Hard-constraint tool to prevent illegal/invalid actions
takeaways.what_they_do: A dedicated legal-moves tool stops the model from ever reasoning about impossible moves, catching a whole class of errors at the tool boundary.
takeaways.evidence_quote: a tool for legal moves... to just prevent it from ever like thinking about something completely illegal

takeaways.technique: Deliberately inject conflicting/diverse signals to improve output quality
takeaways.what_they_do: They feed the agent both engine-best moves and human-plausibility moves plus historical context, so the description covers what humans would actually consider, not just the optimal line.
takeaways.evidence_quote: this kind of conflicting information which we provide by the tools is actually very beneficial

takeaways.technique: Accept redundant tool calls as a known, measurable waste to optimize later
takeaways.what_they_do: They knowingly tolerate the agent re-walking a game twice and list 'redundant tool calls' as an explicit future optimization rather than blocking on it.
takeaways.evidence_quote: redundant tool calls. Sometimes the agent goes through a game like twice or something like that, and yeah, that's obviously stupid

takeaways.technique: Human spot-check sampling with a quantified error rate
takeaways.what_they_do: The operator still watches a sample of auto-generated videos and estimates a defect rate, using failures as signal about which tool call was missed.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the error rate is actually pretty low. So, I would say every 20th um video maybe has a a very weird description
takeaways.numbers: ~1 in 20 videos has a bad description

takeaways.technique: Nightly scheduled batch pipeline with auto-publish and post-hoc takedown
takeaways.what_they_do: A routine runs every night, produces artifacts, and auto-uploads; the human has shifted from pre-approval to after-the-fact takedown of bad outputs.
